name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
At eighteen, applying for my first job, I remember thinking very clearly: not sales. Anything but sales.

I ended up spending the better part of the next twelve years in roles that were, if I'm honest with myself, sales wearing a different job title. Executive assistant to a CEO, coordinating deals I told myself I was just "supporting." Business development. Marketing that somehow always circled back to closing something.

I used to tell people, half joking, that sales just wasn't my thing and I'd rather find something else entirely. I believed it for a long time.

What actually changed wasn't that I suddenly became a closer. I'm still not, and I've made peace with that. What changed is I noticed the thing I kept avoiding was also the thing I was quietly good at every time I got close enough to it: not pitching hard, just being genuinely useful to someone until trust built on its own.

Turns out that's most of what this job actually is. I just needed twelve years and a title with "Account Executive" in it to admit that the thing I ran from was already my thing the whole time.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
A prospect ghosted our onboarding three separate times. Not rude about it, just quiet. Kept meaning to, kept not getting to it.

Then last month, unprompted: "honestly didn't expect to still be using this three months in, but here we are."

I didn't do anything clever to make that happen. I just didn't stop showing up. A casual check-in here, a genuine "hey, this update might actually solve the thing you mentioned" there, never with any edge to it, never making someone feel bad about going quiet the last three times.

I learned this the slow way, years ago, working with agencies where a twelve month sales cycle was completely normal and nobody blinked at it. You stop expecting the yes to arrive on your timeline. You just keep the door open and genuinely mean it every time.

Most sales advice is built around the pitch. Mine is built around what happens for the eleven months after the pitch, when nothing's happening on the surface and you're the only one still paying attention.

The close isn't the moment. It's whatever you did in all the quiet months before it that made someone comfortable enough to come back on their own.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
I have a low hum of needing to be doing something useful, even when there's genuinely nothing urgent happening. A friend once called it main character productivity guilt. Close enough.

The thing that quiets it fastest isn't a productivity system. It's just moving somewhere else. A different café, a different corner of the apartment, once memorably a co-working space with a chair considerably less comfortable than my actual desk chair.

Something about a new environment resets whatever loop is running. I don't fully understand the mechanism. I just know that when I'm stuck, staring at the same wall I've been staring at for three hours, the fix is almost never "push through." It's leave.

I used to feel a little embarrassed admitting that changing my scenery does more for my output than any calendar blocking technique I've tried. It felt like a soft answer to a problem I thought needed a disciplined one.

It's not soft. It's just the actual lever, for me specifically, and I've stopped pretending I should need a more impressive-sounding one.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
Eight years ago I was an executive assistant. Today I build the operating systems that let AI companies scale revenue without their delivery quietly falling apart underneath them.

Nobody plans that specific path. It just accumulated, one operational fire at a time.

As an EA, I ended up owning a CRM migration nobody else wanted to touch, because "just handle it" turned out to include the parts everyone else was avoiding. That migration contributed to a 2.5x revenue year, not because I closed anything myself, but because sales stopped losing deals to bad data.

Years later, running marketing operations at a dev shop, we doubled our profit target in a single year by fixing the boring stuff: the handoffs between sales and delivery, the pricing logic nobody had actually revisited since the company was three people.

Most recently, automating close to 70% of client onboarding at an AI automation company, while revenue tripled around it.

None of these were the exciting part of anyone's job description. I've built an entire career out of being the person who actually goes and fixes the unglamorous connective tissue between departments, the part everyone agrees is a problem and nobody wants to own.

Turns out that's a genuinely valuable thing to be good at.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
Writing has never come easily to me. Neither has being consistent about much of anything creative. I've started, stopped, and quietly abandoned more content plans than I'd like to count.

What I've always had instead is a stubborn refusal to just stop doing something because I'm bad at it.

At eighteen I was convinced sales wasn't my thing. Spent the next decade proving myself wrong by accident, one sales-adjacent job at a time. Karaoke is the same story on a smaller, sillier scale, genuinely not a good singer, and somehow that fact has never once stopped me from getting up there.

There's a version of "find your strengths and only do those" that's quietly bad advice. It sounds efficient. What it actually does is let you avoid the exact things that would eventually become strengths, if you'd just kept doing them badly for long enough to get less bad.

I'm not trying to become a great writer. I'm trying to find whatever version of showing up and saying something real turns out to be mine, the same way I eventually found that in sales despite spending years insisting it wasn't for me.

The skill was never the point. The not-quitting was.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
Wrote our August product update this week, and looking back at the list, none of it is flashy. All of it is stuff people actually asked for.

Instagram Reels now works the same way YouTube Shorts already did: point at one long video, get a week of native clips with subtitles and descriptions already written. Carousels jumped to 20 images. Small thing, kept coming up.

The one I'm personally most into: you can now highlight just the line in a post that isn't landing and regenerate only that part. Before, a weak opening meant rerolling the entire post and losing copy you'd already liked. That always bugged me more than it probably should have.

Link placement is now per platform too. Leave it in-post on X, drop it to the first comment on LinkedIn, because that's genuinely how each platform treats it.

None of this is a headline feature. It's the unglamorous stuff that actually determines whether you keep using a tool six weeks in or quietly drift back to doing it manually. Every one of these came from someone telling us exactly where it slowed them down.

If something in your own workflow still takes longer than it should, that's still the fastest way onto our roadmap. Just tell us.

name: Yuliya Haranok
body:
The best advice in our own automation guide isn't about which tool to use. It's a line about building a kill switch.

Pause all your scheduled content automatically during a natural disaster, a national tragedy, a PR mess, anything where posting on autopilot reads as genuinely tone-deaf. Most brands find out they needed one the exact week they didn't have it.

The other one that stuck with me: don't fully automate everything, especially your one or two main platforms. An 80/20 split, mostly automated, a real slice still written and posted by an actual human in the moment, tends to hold up a lot better than either extreme.

And stagger your post times. If your best window is 9 to 10am, don't schedule for 9:00 sharp. Something like 9:28 reads as a person who happened to post then, not a queue firing on the hour.

None of these are secrets. They're just the specific, slightly boring discipline that separates a brand that automates well from one that automates and then gets quietly weird the one week it actually mattered to sound human.

Automation is supposed to buy you the judgment calls back. Not remove them.
